titulo: Ticket, rule, vehicle — in that order
subtitulo: Buy for the destination, discover validation and transfer rules, then confirm the vehicle before boarding
cena: The ticket is already in your hand, warm from the machine, and it has told you nothing yet about the one rule that decides whether it actually works.
frasePiso: A ticket is not useful until you know where it goes and what must happen before you board.

clique.desconto: Nobody taught you two separate obligation questions. You built both out of one opening, by changing only the action after it.
clique.piso: Next time a ticket machine or a turnstile is in front of you, you won't stand there guessing whether you're missing a step. You'll ask.

steps.pt: No single national transport ritual — paper, card or app, rules vary. Your sequence stays: destination, ticket, rule, platform, vehicle.
Does this transport go downtown?

steps.promptPt: Before buying anything, confirm whether this service goes downtown. Speak now.
steps.pt: Does this transport go downtown?

steps.es: Sí, pero tiene que hacer transbordo.
steps.pt: Yes, but you have to transfer.
steps.tts: Sí, pero tiene que hacer transbordo.

steps.pt: Buy for the destination, not a fixed fare-word — boleto is the useful ticket word here.

steps.promptPt: At the staffed counter, ask for one ticket to downtown. Speak now.
steps.es: Un boleto para el centro, por favor.
steps.pinyin: oon boh-LEH-toh PAH-rah el SEHN-troh por fah-BOR
steps.pt: One ticket to downtown, please.
Here you are.
Ticket in hand, rule still unknown. Tengo que asks the obligation — keep the opening, attach the action.
Do I have to validate the ticket?

steps.promptPt: You have the ticket, but there is a reader before the platform. Ask whether you must validate it. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do I have to validate the ticket?
Yes, at that machine.
Don't decode the machine from a distance — follow the hand, validate, then find the platform if there is one.

steps.promptPt: The ticket is valid, but you still need the platform for this departure. Ask where the platform is. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the platform?
At the back, on the left.
Same opening, new action. The first answer said transfer — ask whether it applies to this journey.

steps.promptPt: At the platform, ask whether you have to make a transfer on the way downtown. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do I have to transfer?
Yes, once.
Last check happens at the door. Confirm this bus goes there — the line number can stay on the sign.

steps.promptPt: The bus arrives at the platform. Before boarding, confirm that this vehicle goes to the Historic Centre. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: EHS-teh ow-toh-BOOS bah al SEHN-troh ees-TOH-ree-koh
steps.pt: Does this bus go to the Historic Centre?
Yes. Board, please.

steps.promptPt: You need the staffed window, not a machine. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the ticket window?

steps.promptPt: This one is full. Ask whether a later one exists. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is there another bus later?

steps.promptPt: You are travelling with someone. Ask at the window. Speak now.
steps.pinyin: meh dah dohs boh-LEH-tohs por fah-BOR
steps.pt: Can I have two tickets, please?

steps.es: ¿Tengo que validar el boleto? ¿Tengo que hacer transbordo?
steps.pinyin: TEHN-goh keh bah-lee-DAHR el boh-LEH-toh. TEHN-goh keh ah-SEHR trahns-BOR-doh
steps.pt: Shadow the obligation opening with two different actions.
steps.tts: ¿Tengo que validar el boleto? ¿Tengo que hacer transbordo?

steps.pt: B09 complete. Destination, boleto, validation rule, platform, transfer, confirm the vehicle — the sequence is your job.

aprofundar.titulo: Discover the rule; do not import one

secoes.corpo: Boleto is the working Mexican ticket word in this course. The product behind it may be paper, card or app, so ask for the destination rather than assuming a specific fare product.
Use the same opening to discover an obligation.

exemplos.pt: Do I have to validate the ticket?

secoes.corpo: Read the line, fare or platform from the display and point when needed. Productive number performance is not the price of entering the correct vehicle.
The first destination question protects the purchase. The second protects the boarding. Repetition here closes two different risks.

permissao: You are allowed to ask the same kind of question twice in five minutes. Checking the destination before buying and again before boarding is not you being forgetful or anxious — it is the only way to catch a transfer or a validation rule that a system with no national standard was never going to volunteer.
espelho: Anyone who has ever tapped an unfamiliar transit card at the wrong reader or boarded the wrong platform in their own city knows this exact uncertainty — Mexico's lack of one national ticketing ritual isn't a harder version of the problem, it's the same problem any traveller has already solved before, just with local words attached.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You board a bus or train confidently because the destination matches, and partway through the ride you realise everyone else validated a ticket or scanned a card in a way you never did.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I got lucky, or the rules here are unpredictable and impossible to learn in advance.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Mexico has no single national transport system, so validation, transfers and even the ticket product itself change by city and operator — the unpredictability is real and structural, not a sign you missed something anyone else would have known.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask ¿tengo que validar el boleto? before you commit to a platform, the same way you already asked whether the vehicle goes to your destination.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You catch the local rule while there is still time to act on it, instead of discovering it from a fellow passenger's reaction mid-journey.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not a reason to ask about every system feature in advance — the two questions cover validation and transfer specifically because those are the two obligations that actually change trip outcomes.
